\subsection{The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses}
\seclabel{revival-meet}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{more-specific-rule}; \secref{overloading-static-params};
\secref{overloading-coercion-resolution}; and, in a draft build, the proposed
features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] Where the Meet Rule for functions, or for functional methods,
asks for a declaration on the intersection of two parameter types, declarations
whose parameter types are each a subtype of both and together cover the
intersection also satisfy it, every pair of those declarations satisfying the
rules in turn; the case does not apply to the condition on the types from which
the two parameter types define coercions.
A box at the rule answers the draft note that asks what the intersection of two
declarations is; the Meet Rule of \secref{overloading-static-params} gains the
same case, with a box.
The Meet Rule's example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, and that $f(V)$
is applicable to and more specific for any call at run time to which $f(S)$ and
$f(T)$ are applicable.
\secref{principles-overloading} says that a static call whose argument's static
that extends both unlisted does, is not a static error: it runs the declaration
that covers its value, and, where those declarations and every declaration more
specific than them that the call may run have no static parameters, its type is
the intersection of the return types of its most specific declarations.
The compiled type checker departs from this in four ways: it types such a call
by the intersection only in a family none of whose declarations has static
parameters, and otherwise by one of its most specific declarations (row~543 of
the revival's gap ledger); its code generator stops at a method call on a value
of such a type (row~540); it refuses the case for declarations with static
parameters (row~546); and its verdict on a trait between the two that provides
both declarations of a functional method can depend on the components it
compiled before (row~547).
The Meet Rule for dotted methods keeps its form, asking for a declaration on the
intersection (\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft's rules are unchanged, the cases being
added after them.

convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression

type is not a subtype of any floating-point type.  Fortress supports
the automatic conversion of values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and of integer
numerals, to the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (the technical term for this kind of automatic

\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} explicitly (\secref{basic-rationals}).  In
this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
\revision{revival-int-float}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point

type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes,
such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type,
or the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}); whether inference may give such a parameter
\TYP{BottomType}, which programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}), is
left open;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
an argument of another call, an expression that a local declaration precedes in
a block, an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase}
expression, the body of a \KWD{for} loop, or a call written by loose
juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x};
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-inference}{For a type parameter that only the return type
mentions and that the expected type does not fix, the compiled type checker binds the parameter to \TYP{BottomType},
except that it refuses a call that has no expected type when the parameter is
declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}; the interpreter erases such a parameter of a function
to \TYP{BottomType}, and leaves a generic method's uninstantiated (rows~21, 424, 425 and~447 of the revival's gap ledger).
Whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
below.
Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
parameter.}

\note{ \begin{itemize}
 \item
 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
 \end{itemize}
}

content.content:
\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
contradict is known to be unrevised.
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter left unrevised, the
sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters were
inferred before the applicability of a declaration was checked and before
declarations were compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the
rule of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound
\TYP{Any}, are revised with the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading},
\secref{revival-bound}). The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).
The item of the list of \chapref{type-inference} of what it does not yet
describe on a static parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type
fixes, and its box on the compiled type checker's binding of such a parameter,
are not yet revised to the rule of \secref{resolving-overloading} by which a
dispatched declaration is instantiated (\secref{revival-dispatch}).
The instance of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of a declaration that a call
reaches only by dispatch, where nothing fixes it at run time, is not described;
the rule of \secref{resolving-overloading} is for type parameters (row~446 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The sentence of \secref{where-clauses} that a \KWD{where}-clause variable may
not appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause also refuses a
variable that a constraint fixes to one type; whether it is to be narrowed is
not settled.
The Meet Rule for dotted methods (\secref{more-specific-rule}) asks for a
declaration on the intersection of two parameter types; whether declarations
that together cover the intersection satisfy it too is not settled.
The type of a static call whose argument's static type stands between two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, where its most specific declarations, or a
declaration more specific than them that the call may run, have static
parameters, is not given (\secref{revival-meet}).
Whether two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments
at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out is not settled: the
compiled type checker takes them to exclude where the static argument that the
two parameter types force is a named type that fails the bound, and not where
it would reason through the ancestors of the parameter types
(\secref{overloading-static-params}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

A count of the programs a change reaches, when a decision needs one, is the planner's probe, taken before the record is written. A one-time count of changed interpreter outputs is asked for only where a decision of Pavol's names it for that rung (rows 330 and the numeral switch's Q-walk, rung Q's measurement), one edit pass against one base pass the coordinator starts before the launch; the record's section 7 holds no copy of the manifest, which `plan-<n>/manifest/` generates.
+A record asks a rung for no corpus-wide output comparison, no ladder 'before', no microGPT check, no specification build log and no whole-suite run. The prefix allows one whole-suite run, at most once per code state in a rung's chain, and only to a rung whose edit changes the checker's or walk's source (Java or Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`): the compiler and library tracks for the checker, the interpreter suite for walk. The worker runs it after its last edit, and a repair round after its own, with the verdict lines, command and commit in `REPORT.md`; the skeptic reads that result and does not run it again. Every other rung leaves the suites' verdict to the gate. A stop the record reserves that turns on a test's verdict (a verdict changed other than the rung's own, a set walk loaded refused after) is judged by the gate on the merged tree, and the record says so rather than asking a rung for a suite run (climb batch 7b's review, finding 5, approved 2026-09-30). In 7b rung C's chain ran the compiler and library tracks whole five times, twice on an unchanged tree, about 8 minutes of the box each, and found nothing its targeted runs had not. Rung W ran the interpreter suite once
-New: a `run_bg`/`wait_for` pair at five-second granularity (item 7); a worker's scratch goes under its worktree's `tmp/<slug>/` and is never committed (post-mortem 2026-09-29); `ant` is never piped through `tail` (item i). +Since 2026-09-30 the skeptic's brief carries the worker's `reportText` again, under a line of its own after the worker's structured report (climb batch 7b's review, finding 4). The post-mortem of 2026-09-29 had taken the texts out, on the premise that `REPORT.md` is on the branch. The harness refused the worker's write of `REPORT.md` in four of batch 7b's five worker passes. W's skeptic could not check the provenance block, and the skeptics of C, S and L searched the run's transcripts for the text. The script cannot see the branch, so it passes the text whenever the worker returned one. The line says that where the branch carries the file, the file is the report and this is its copy; where it does not, the text is the report, and the checks of `REPORT.md` are checks of it. It costs the report's size on every first and second skeptic, 27 to 59 KB in batch 7b, and duplicates the file where the write went through. `recordText` stays out: the skeptic reads `record.md` for check 8 only, and the gather writes it from the journal.

+### A usage limit stops the run and decides nothing (2026-09-30)
+
+The retry was built for one agent that dies. A usage limit stops every agent at once, and the script read what followed as decisions. At 02:16 UTC on 2026-09-30 climb batch 7b's run (`wf_61521277-479`) met the account's weekly limit. `agent()` returned null for every agent from then on, and the harness logged `[skeptic:C] failed: You've hit your weekly limit` beside each. `callAgent` ran each role three times within seconds. The stage read each null skeptic as a refusal and each null judge as a drop, marked C, S and L dropped, and started the gather with W alone. The gather failed on the limit too, and that alone kept W from landing without the other three (`reviews/batch-7b-review.md`, section 3 and finding 1). The resume at 04:45 worked, because the journal records an empty attempt as failed.
+
+Since then the run stops, and decides nothing, in two cases (`callAgent`, and the comment above it, "A stop that decides nothing"):
+- `agent()` throws an error whose message names a usage or rate limit (`LIMIT_ERROR`: "usage limit", "rate limit", "weekly limit", "hit your … limit", "too many requests", 429 and the like). The role is not run again.
+- A rung worker, a skeptic or a judge comes back with nothing after its three attempts. This covers the worker's first pass, its resumption after a stop and its repair round, the first and second skeptic, the judge on a stop and on a refusal, and the review's and the gate's judge; their calls pass `needed`. The workers joined the same day, on the coordinator's reading of Pavol's approval: a rung whose worker dies at a limit is a rung the limit would otherwise count dead. A null does not say why the agent died, and 7b's limit came back as null, so this is the case that would have stopped 7b.
+
+Once stopped, `callAgent` throws at the head of every attempt without starting an agent. A stage of the scatter that throws drops its rung to null, as the harness's `pipeline()` does. Below the scatter the script throws before it reads any rung's state, so no rung is marked dropped, withheld or not landed, and the gather does not start. On the merged tree the thrown error ends the run where it stands. The error and one log line say why, that nothing was decided, and how to resume: `resumeFromRunId` with the same script and the same args, once the cause is gone. The finished agents come back from the journal, and the stopped role runs again.
+
+The script has no clock and cannot wait out a limit, so a clean stop is the whole fix. A limit that comes back as null still gets its three immediate attempts, since a null cannot be told from a death. At a limit those attempts are refused at once and write nothing. The gather, the review, the gate, the commit and a repair on the merged tree that come back with nothing, with no limit error thrown, keep their paths: gather unresolved, `review-missing.1`, the gate run once more, not landed, `review-unrepaired.1`. A rung is never marked `worker-died` now. A worker that returns nothing stops the run, even when the cause is a death rather than a limit; resuming then runs it again. Without the workers, one case stayed open. A limit that comes back as null while the last rung's worker runs alone, every other chain done, marked that rung `worker-died`. The gather then landed the others without it.
+
+
+Climb batch 7b's review, finding 1 ("A usage limit stops the run and decides nothing", above), was checked with nothing launched and no build, by `coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js`. That is the scenario checker, committed with the fix. It is `checkn.js`'s successor, removed from the tree at `ab067d9b6`. It expected the second review, so it could not run on this script; the checker carries instead the 22 paths and one resume of the script review's `scen.js` (`postmortem-2026-09-29/script-review.md`, "The scenarios run"). A10 to A13 carry the landings that night's fixes gave them. The code outside the MANIFEST block is the script's; the block is batch 7b's, from `811053f15`, since the scenarios name its rungs. On the script before the change, the 22 scenarios other than A6 pass. A6, a gate judge that returns nothing three times, then ended "gate red, judge did not order a repair". L1, 7b's weekly limit as a null from C's skeptic on, replays 7b's sequence: C's judge called, C, L and S not landed, the gather started with W alone. After the change all 27 pass. A6 stops, as does L1 after `skeptic:C`'s three attempts, with no judge and no gather. L2, a limit error thrown at C's sk
+
+Finding 4, the report's text in the skeptic's brief, was checked by the same checker. Every skeptic in every scenario now carries the worker's report under its line and not its record. On the script before the change that check fails at each skeptic, 98 times over its 27 scenarios.
+
+Finding 5, the whole-suite rule, was checked the same way. Every brief of every scenario carries the prefix's rule and the recovery text on logs, and every skeptic's carries its sentence on reading the run's result. 27 scenarios pass. Not measured: an agent taking the rule.
+
+Finding 9, the worktree the worker makes, was checked the same way: every brief carries the command, and none says the build was copied in. 27 scenarios pass.
+
+The rung worker's calls with `needed` (finding 1, extended the same day) were checked the same way. L5 is the limit as a null at the last rung's worker, with W, C and L done. It stops after `rung:S`'s three attempts, with no gather. A19, a worker that returns nothing three times, stops where it was marked `worker-died`. On the script before the change both fail. All 28 scenarios pass, and the parse checks pass.

def reason_problems(rid):
    out = []
    for k, r in REASONS[rid]:
        if not r or not r.strip():
            out.append((k, 'no reason'))
        elif '\n' in r or '`' in r or any(ord(c) > 127 for c in r):
            out.append((k, 'a reason is one ASCII line with no backtick'))
        elif not r.endswith('.') or len(r) > 240:
            out.append((k, 'a reason ends with a full stop and is at most 240 characters'))
    return out

            if r.returncode or probs:
